sections.section_title: The Memory Wall and Roofline Diagnosis

focus_areas: iron law of ML performance and bottleneck decomposition
GPU memory hierarchy energy and latency physics
widening gap and ridge point evolution across hardware generations
roofline model and operational arithmetic intensity of ML workloads
rationale.question_strategy: Test core physical limits and diagnostic invariants before diving into specific serving or compiler mechanisms: iron law Amdahl math, ridge point shifts across GPU generations, and memory hierarchy energy ladders.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with iron law bottleneck decomposition math, progress to hardware generational ridge point analysis, and end with the physics and power consequences of off-chip vs on-chip data movement.
rationale.integration: Connects foundational hardware acceleration and memory hierarchy concepts from earlier chapters to the performance engineering diagnostic equation.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Foundational section establishing the governing performance equation, memory wall physics, and roofline diagnosis.

questions.question: A training step's wall-clock time is decomposed via the iron law of ML performance into 60% memory traffic ($D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW}$), 30% compute execution ($O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}})$), and 10% dispatch and latency overhead ($L_{\text{lat}}$). A hardware upgrade doubles the GPU's peak dense FP16 compute ($R_{\text{peak}}$) while leaving memory bandwidth ($\text{BW}$) and software latency ($L_{\text{lat}}$) unchanged. What is the maximum theoretical speedup this upgrade can achieve on this workload?
choices: 2.00x speedup, because doubling peak compute throughput halves the overall execution time of matrix multiplication operations
1.67x speedup, because the 30% compute fraction and 10% latency fraction are both accelerated by the faster clock frequency
Approximately 1.18x speedup (a 15% reduction in step time), because doubling compute only reduces the 30% compute slice to 15% while the 70% non-compute time remains unchanged
1.43x speedup, because the memory-bound portion is compressed by the faster arithmetic execution units
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Approximately 1.18x speedup (a 15% reduction in step time), because doubling compute only reduces the 30% compute slice to 15% while the 70% non-compute time remains unchanged. Under the iron law ($T = D_{\text{vol}}/\text{BW} + O/(R_{\text{peak}} \cdot \eta_{\text{hw}}) + L_{\text{lat}}$), doubling $R_{\text{peak}}$ only affects the compute term, halving it from 0.30 to 0.15 of the baseline time. The new normalized time is $0.60 + 0.15 + 0.10 = 0.85$, yielding a speedup of $1.0 / 0.85 \approx 1.18\times$. Expecting a 2.0x speedup commits the classic Amdahl's law fallacy by ignoring that 70% of execution is governed by memory bandwidth and latency, while the other choices incorrectly assume compute hardware improvements accelerate memory transfers or fixed software dispatch overhead.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the iron law of ML performance to calculate the theoretical speedup of targeted hardware upgrades under Amdahl's law constraints

questions.question: An operation has an arithmetic intensity of 200 FLOP/byte. On an NVIDIA V100 (peak FP16 = 125 TFLOP/s, HBM BW = 0.9 TB/s, ridge point = 139 FLOP/byte) and an H100 (peak FP16 = 989 TFLOP/s, HBM BW = 3.35 TB/s, ridge point = 295 FLOP/byte), how does the workload's operational bottleneck shift, and what is the systems implication?
choices: It shifts from memory-bound on V100 to compute-bound on H100, because the H100 has nearly 4x higher HBM memory bandwidth
It remains compute-bound on both GPUs because an arithmetic intensity of 200 FLOP/byte is strictly higher than any typical transformer layer intensity

It shifts from compute-bound on V100 to memory-bound on H100, meaning memory optimization techniques (fusion, tiling, quantization) become critical on H100 even though compute scheduling was sufficient on V100
It remains memory-bound on both GPUs because the arithmetic intensity of an operation is fixed by hardware architecture rather than software algorithm
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. It shifts from compute-bound on V100 to memory-bound on H100, meaning memory optimization techniques (fusion, tiling, quantization) become critical on H100 even though compute scheduling was sufficient on V100. The ridge point $I_{\text{ridge}} = R_{\text{peak}} / \text{BW}$ rose from ~139 FLOP/byte on V100 to ~295 FLOP/byte on H100 because compute throughput grew ($7.9\times$) much faster than memory bandwidth ($3.7\times$). An operation at 200 FLOP/byte sits above the V100 ridge point (compute-bound) but falls below the H100 ridge point (memory-bound). The other options miscalculate the relative position against the ridge point or falsely claim arithmetic intensity is an intrinsic hardware constant rather than an algorithmic property.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate how generational shifts in hardware balance points change the active performance bottleneck of ML workloads

questions.question: On an H100 GPU, accessing data from on-chip SRAM (L1/shared memory) costs approximately 0.5 pJ per access, while fetching the same data from off-chip HBM costs roughly 640 pJ (a ~1280x ratio). What is the primary thermodynamic and performance consequence of repeatedly streaming intermediate tensors through HBM rather than retaining them in on-chip SRAM?
choices: Streaming through HBM causes numerical drift and precision loss because DRAM capacitors lose charge over multi-nanosecond round-trips
SRAM access draws higher total power because operating at higher clock frequencies increases dynamic capacitance dissipation beyond HBM interface PHYs
Off-chip transfers bypass the L2 cache entirely, preventing the GPU memory management unit from performing virtual address translation

Streaming through HBM dissipates tens of watts per GPU in memory interface power alone and stalls SMs for hundreds of nanoseconds per access, whereas SRAM access completes in 20–30 clock cycles at sub-picojoule energy
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Streaming through HBM dissipates tens of watts per GPU in memory interface power alone and stalls SMs for hundreds of nanoseconds per access, whereas SRAM access completes in 20–30 clock cycles at sub-picojoule energy. Moving data off-chip across longer wires to HBM stacks costs ~10 pJ/byte (~640 pJ per 64-byte transaction), drawing 35–50 W per GPU solely across memory interfaces at full bandwidth and introducing ~300 ns latency bubbles. Keeping intermediate activations in on-chip SRAM cuts access energy by over 1000x and latency to ~20 ns. The other options invent false physical claims about DRAM precision drift, misrepresent SRAM power scaling, or misdescribe GPU virtual memory translation.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the energy and latency trade-offs across levels of the GPU memory hierarchy

sections.section_title: Serving Regimes: Batch Size and Prefill-Decode

focus_areas: batch size scaling of arithmetic intensity
KV cache capacity limits and serving economics
PagedAttention fragmentation elimination
prefill versus decode bottleneck decomposition
napkin math for LLM decode token generation rates
rationale.question_strategy: Probe the distinct structural regimes of LLM serving: how batch size amortizes weight reads, why prefill and decode exhibit opposing bottlenecks, and how memory capacity constrains batch scaling.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the prefill-decode phase bottleneck dichotomy, move to PagedAttention memory mechanics vs quantization, and conclude with exact roofline napkin math for batch-1 decode token generation.
rationale.integration: Bridges roofline diagnosis with practical LLM inference serving dynamics and memory capacity constraints.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core section introducing the dual serving phases, batch size arithmetic intensity scaling, and KV cache capacity ceilings.

questions.question: A production LLM serving cluster processes requests through two distinct phases: prompt prefill ($S=1024$ tokens) and autoregressive token decode ($B=1$). How do their operational bottlenecks and arithmetic intensities fundamentally differ?
choices: Prefill computes all prompt tokens in parallel with high arithmetic intensity ($I \approx 1024$ FLOP/byte in FP16), making it compute-bound on Tensor Cores, while batch-1 decode streams the entire weight matrix for every single emitted token ($I \approx 1$ FLOP/byte), making it memory-bound on HBM bandwidth

Prefill is memory-bound because loading the large input prompt consumes all available HBM bandwidth, while decode is compute-bound because generating new tokens requires solving an autoregressive search problem
Both phases are equally compute-bound because transformer layers execute the exact same matrix multiplication dimensions regardless of sequence length or batch size
Both phases are overhead-bound because token sampling and Python dispatch latency exceed GPU kernel execution time for all prompt lengths
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Prefill computes all prompt tokens in parallel with high arithmetic intensity ($I \approx 1024$ FLOP/byte in FP16), making it compute-bound on Tensor Cores, while batch-1 decode streams the entire weight matrix for every single emitted token ($I \approx 1$ FLOP/byte), making it memory-bound on HBM bandwidth. During prefill, the forward pass processes $S=1024$ tokens simultaneously, creating a large $[S, d_{\text{model}}] \times [d_{\text{model}}, d_{\text{model}}]$ GEMM where weight bytes are reused across all 1024 tokens, pushing arithmetic intensity well above the H100 ridge point (~295 FLOP/byte). In contrast, batch-1 decode performs a vector-matrix multiply $[1, d_{\text{model}}] \times [d_{\text{model}}, d_{\text{model}}]$ per step, reading the entire parameter matrix to produce one token ($I \approx 1$ FLOP/byte). The other options misclassify the phase bottlenecks or ignore the structural difference between parallel matrix-matrix multiplication and sequential vector-matrix streaming.
questions.learning_objective: Differentiate the operational bottlenecks and arithmetic intensities of LLM prefill and decode serving phases

questions.question: An engineering team is evaluating memory optimizations to increase serving concurrency for a 70B model. An engineer proposes that PagedAttention and KV cache quantization are redundant since both are designed to expand maximum batch size. Why is this reasoning flawed from a systems architecture perspective?
choices: PagedAttention is an optimization exclusively for prompt prefill, whereas KV cache quantization only operates during speculative decoding

PagedAttention eliminates internal and external memory fragmentation by allocating fixed-size page blocks on demand, whereas KV cache quantization reduces the byte footprint per cached token; the two techniques attack orthogonal sources of memory waste and compound together
PagedAttention increases arithmetic intensity by storing KV cache in on-chip registers, whereas quantization only reduces PCIe transfer latency
KV cache quantization eliminates the need for virtual memory paging because quantized INT8 tensors do not require contiguous memory buffers
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. PagedAttention eliminates internal and external memory fragmentation by allocating fixed-size page blocks on demand, whereas KV cache quantization reduces the byte footprint per cached token; the two techniques attack orthogonal sources of memory waste and compound together. PagedAttention solves the virtual memory management problem (recovering the 60–80% of HBM wasted by preallocating contiguous buffers for worst-case sequence lengths). KV cache quantization (e.g., FP16 to INT8) reduces the actual payload per cached key and value by 2x. Operating together, PagedAttention ensures that nearly 100% of allocated KV memory holds active tokens, while quantization doubles the token capacity of that allocated space. The alternative choices misstate the scope of PagedAttention, invent false register-caching claims, or misunderstand memory allocator physics.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish memory fragmentation recovery from byte-per-entry compression in KV cache scaling strategies

questions.question: A 70B parameter LLM is sharded across 8 H100 GPUs (each with 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth and 989 TFLOP/s peak FP16 compute) using tensor parallelism. In FP16, each GPU holds ~17.5 GB of weights. At batch size 1, assuming pure weight-streaming with negligible KV cache and communication overhead, what is the theoretical maximum token generation rate for the model, and what fraction of the H100's peak FP16 compute is utilized?
choices: Approximately 1,530 tokens/second with ~3.2% compute utilization, because tensor parallelism across 8 GPUs multiplies token generation throughput by 8x
Approximately 56 tokens/second with ~50% compute utilization, because FP16 Tensor Cores operate at half-clock speed during autoregressive decoding
Approximately 191 tokens/second with ~85% compute utilization, because memory bandwidth saturation implies near-peak arithmetic core engagement
Approximately 191 tokens/second with less than 0.4% compute utilization, because token emission is strictly bottlenecked by streaming 17.5 GB of weights across 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Approximately 191 tokens/second with less than 0.4% compute utilization, because token emission is strictly bottlenecked by streaming 17.5 GB of weights across 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth. Each decode step requires loading the GPU's weight shard: $T_{\text{decode}} = 17.5\text{ GB} / 3.35\text{ TB/s} \approx 5.22\text{ ms per token}$, yielding $1 / 0.00522 \approx 191.4\text{ tokens/s}$. FLOPs per step per GPU = $2 \times 8.75\text{B} = 17.5\text{ GFLOP}$. Achieved compute rate = $17.5\text{ GFLOP} / 5.22\text{ ms} \approx 3.35\text{ TFLOP/s}$, which is only $3.35 / 989 \approx 0.34\%$ ($<0.4\%$) of the H100's peak FP16 capacity. Tensor parallelism divides the model weights across GPUs but does not multiply batch-1 token throughput because each step remains synchronized. High memory utilization (MBU) coexists with near-zero compute utilization (MFU) in memory-bound decode.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate theoretical token throughput and compute utilization limits for memory-bound LLM decoding using roofline napkin math

focus_areas: kernel launch overhead and launch-bound execution
HBM intermediate tensor traffic in unfused layers
fusion taxonomy: element-wise, reduction, and operator-specific
CUDA Graphs determinism and replay constraints
FlashAttention online softmax invariant and SRAM tiling
rationale.question_strategy: Test concrete systems mechanisms that reduce data movement and dispatch latency: unfused HBM traffic calculations, FlashAttention online softmax rescaling mechanics, and CUDA Graphs determinism rules.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with quantifying unfused intermediate memory traffic, move to the mathematical invariants of FlashAttention's online softmax, and finish with execution constraints of CUDA Graphs.
rationale.integration: Builds directly on memory hierarchy physics and roofline arithmetic intensity by showing how fusion eliminates round-trips to HBM.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Critical technical section introducing kernel fusion categories, dispatch elimination via CUDA Graphs, and FlashAttention.

questions.question: In an unfused transformer block, the sequence $Y = \text{LayerNorm}(\text{GELU}(XW + b))$ executes as three separate GPU kernels. For a hidden dimension of 4096 and batch size of 2048 in FP16, each intermediate activation tensor occupies 16 MB. How much intermediate HBM read/write traffic is generated across 80 layers in an unfused forward pass, and how does operator fusion eliminate it?
choices: It generates 16 MB of intermediate HBM traffic per layer (~1.3 GB across 80 layers); fusion eliminates parameter loading by caching weights in shared memory
It generates 64 MB of intermediate HBM traffic per layer (~5.1 GB across 80 layers); a fused kernel retains intermediates in registers/SRAM, cutting HBM round-trips from 6 to 2 per layer block
It generates 128 MB of intermediate HBM traffic per layer (~10.2 GB across 80 layers); fusion compresses activations to 4-bit integers in global memory
It generates 0 MB of intermediate HBM traffic because PyTorch automatically merges all sequential Python functions into a single CUDA thread block
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. It generates 64 MB of intermediate HBM traffic per layer (~5.1 GB across 80 layers); a fused kernel retains intermediates in registers/SRAM, cutting HBM round-trips from 6 to 2 per layer block. In unfused execution, the GEMM writes intermediate $Z_1$ (16 MB) to HBM, GELU reads $Z_1$ (16 MB) and writes $Z_2$ (16 MB) to HBM, and LayerNorm reads $Z_2$ (16 MB) and writes final $Y$ (16 MB) to HBM. The two intermediate tensors alone generate $16 + 16 + 16 + 16 = 64\text{ MB}$ of redundant HBM traffic per layer ($64\text{ MB} \times 80 = 5.12\text{ GB}$ total) across 6 round-trip transfers. A fused kernel keeps $Z_1$ and $Z_2$ in on-chip registers or shared memory, reading inputs once and writing output $Y$ once (2 HBM transfers). The other choices miscalculate intermediate traffic, misrepresent fusion as weight caching or quantization, or assume eager PyTorch fuses operations automatically.
questions.learning_objective: Quantify the off-chip HBM memory traffic eliminated by operator fusion in multi-layer neural networks

questions.question: FlashAttention computes exact attention within on-chip SRAM by processing $Q, K, V$ in tiles. When processing a new key-value tile $t$, why is the rescaling step (multiplying the previous running output accumulator by $e^{m_{\text{old}} - m_{\text{new}}}$) mathematically necessary before accumulating the new tile's contribution?
choices: Because GPU shared memory loses floating-point precision over time, requiring periodic renormalization against zero
Because CUDA warp shuffle instructions require all intermediate accumulator values to be powers of two

Because softmax requires normalizing exponents by the global maximum; if the new tile reveals a larger local maximum ($m_{\text{new}} > m_{\text{old}}$), prior partial sums computed with $m_{\text{old}}$ must be scaled down to maintain consistent normalization
Because rescaling prevents underflow in the value matrix $V$ before it is written back to HBM
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Because softmax requires normalizing exponents by the global maximum; if the new tile reveals a larger local maximum ($m_{\text{new}} > m_{\text{old}}$), prior partial sums computed with $m_{\text{old}}$ must be scaled down to maintain consistent normalization. Numerically stable softmax computes $\text{softmax}(s_i) = e^{s_i - m} / \sum_j e^{s_j - m}$ where $m = \max_j s_j$. When tiling attention across SRAM blocks, the global maximum is unknown upfront. If tile $t$ contains a score larger than the running maximum ($m_{\text{new}} > m_{\text{old}}$), multiplying earlier accumulated partial outputs by $e^{m_{\text{old}} - m_{\text{new}}}$ algebraically fixes up their normalization without ever materializing the quadratic $S \times S$ score matrix in HBM. The other choices invent false mechanisms about SRAM decay, warp shuffle constraints, or value matrix underflow.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how online softmax rescaling enables tiled attention algorithms to compute mathematically exact results within fixed-size SRAM

questions.question: A serving team attempts to apply CUDA Graphs across their entire LLM inference pipeline. They observe substantial throughput gains during repetitive token decode, but enabling CUDA Graphs on the prompt prefill phase causes runtime crashes and latency regressions. What fundamental system constraint explains this behavior?
choices: CUDA Graphs require strict determinism (identical operation sequences, static tensor shapes, and fixed memory addresses across replays); repetitive decode with fixed batch and token shapes satisfies this, whereas variable-length prompt prefill triggers expensive graph recaptures
CUDA Graphs are only compatible with single-precision FP32 arithmetic and fail on FP16 Tensor Core kernels used during prefill
CUDA Graphs disable all asynchronous GPU execution, forcing the CPU to synchronize after every individual matrix multiplication
The NVIDIA driver restricts CUDA Graphs to single-layer models with fewer than 10 total kernel launches
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. CUDA Graphs require strict determinism (identical operation sequences, static tensor shapes, and fixed memory addresses across replays); repetitive decode with fixed batch and token shapes satisfies this, whereas variable-length prompt prefill triggers expensive graph recaptures. A CUDA Graph captures a static execution graph once during warmup and replays it with a single CPU-to-GPU launch command (~5–10 $\mu$s). If tensor shapes change (as happens with dynamic prompt lengths in prefill), the recorded graph is invalid, forcing a full graph recapture that takes milliseconds and wipes out all launch savings. Decode iterations, which repeatedly execute identical operations on fixed single-token shapes, perfectly match CUDA Graph determinism constraints. The other options misstate precision support, synchronization behavior, or driver limitations.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the architectural constraints and execution determinism requirements of CUDA Graphs in LLM serving

focus_areas: outlier feature suppression in LLMs
block-wise quantization metadata overhead
post-training quantization algorithms: AWQ, GPTQ, SmoothQuant, LLM.int8()
weight-only versus weight-activation quantization regimes
the precision dividend and KV cache batch scaling economics
rationale.question_strategy: Test the trade-offs between numerical representation, outlier handling mechanisms, hardware execution modes, and KV cache serving capacity.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with outlier-handling mechanics across PTQ schemes, advance to workload matching between weight-only and weight-activation regimes, and finish with KV cache capacity economics.
rationale.integration: Links numerical precision choices directly to memory bandwidth relief, Tensor Core acceleration, and serving batch capacity.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core section detailing quantization algorithms, outlier preservation techniques, and memory capacity expansion.

questions.question: Large language models develop emergent outlier features (hidden dimensions with magnitudes up to 20x larger than typical values in ~0.1% of channels) that destroy accuracy under uniform per-tensor quantization. Which of the following correctly pairs a post-training quantization (PTQ) method with its systems mechanism for handling outliers?
choices: SmoothQuant applies a per-channel scaling transformation that divides activations by a smoothing factor and multiplies weights by the same factor, migrating quantization difficulty to weights and enabling uniform W8A8 INT8 Tensor Core execution
LLM.int8() compresses all outlier features into 1-bit representations while running the remaining normal features in FP32
AWQ computes a full second-order inverse Hessian matrix across all model layers to redistribute outlier quantization noise to unimportant weights
GPTQ dynamically routes activation outliers to CPU DRAM during runtime execution while keeping weights in GPU HBM
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. SmoothQuant applies a per-channel scaling transformation that divides activations by a smoothing factor and multiplies weights by the same factor, migrating quantization difficulty to weights and enabling uniform W8A8 INT8 Tensor Core execution. Activation outliers are channel-specific; by scaling activations down by per-channel factor $s$ and scaling weights up by $s$, the mathematical operation $Y = (X \cdot \text{diag}(s)^{-1}) \cdot (\text{diag}(s) \cdot W)$ is preserved while smoothing the activation dynamic range so both weights and activations can be quantized to INT8. LLM.int8() splits outliers into an FP16 GEMM at runtime rather than 1-bit; AWQ uses activation magnitudes to protect salient channels without computing Hessians; and GPTQ uses layer-wise inverse Hessian reconstruction during calibration without routing activations to CPU DRAM.
questions.learning_objective: Compare post-training quantization schemes and their mechanisms for mitigating outlier feature degradation in large language models

questions.question: A performance engineer is choosing between weight-only INT4 quantization (with on-the-fly FP16 dequantization in registers) and weight-activation FP8 quantization (W8A8) for two workloads: (1) single-user interactive decode ($B=1$), and (2) high-throughput batched serving ($B=128$). Which pairing best aligns with the underlying hardware bottlenecks?
choices: Deploy W8A8 FP8 for $B=1$ because FP8 Tensor Cores double memory bandwidth, and deploy weight-only INT4 for $B=128$ because INT4 weights eliminate KV cache memory
Deploy weight-only INT4 for both workloads because 4-bit integers always provide higher arithmetic throughput than 8-bit floating point units

Deploy weight-only INT4 for $B=1$ because decode is memory-bound (halving weight bytes directly cuts latency), and deploy W8A8 FP8 for $B=128$ because batched decode is compute-bound (FP8 Tensor Cores deliver 2x higher peak TFLOP/s)
Deploy W8A8 FP8 for both workloads because activation quantization is required for all autoregressive decoding steps regardless of batch size
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Deploy weight-only INT4 for $B=1$ because decode is memory-bound (halving weight bytes directly cuts latency), and deploy W8A8 FP8 for $B=128$ because batched decode is compute-bound (FP8 Tensor Cores deliver 2x higher peak TFLOP/s). At batch size 1, decode execution time is dominated by reading weights from HBM; compressing weights from FP16 to INT4 reduces HBM traffic by 4x and directly speeds up the step even though arithmetic runs in FP16 after dequantization. At batch size 128, large GEMM dimensions raise arithmetic intensity into the compute-bound regime; weight-activation FP8 enables FP8 Tensor Cores, delivering roughly 2x higher dense arithmetic throughput ($R_{\text{peak}}$) that weight-only INT4 cannot provide. The other options misstate hardware capabilities (Tensor Cores do not increase memory bandwidth; INT4 weight-only does not compress KV cache; activation quantization is optional for decode).
questions.learning_objective: Select optimal quantization strategies across memory-bound and compute-bound operating points

questions.question: On an 8-GPU node of 80 GB H100s serving a 70B model, quantizing weights from FP16 (17.5 GB/GPU) to INT4 (4.4 GB/GPU) and the KV cache from FP16 (0.168 GB/request/GPU) to INT8 (0.084 GB/request/GPU) expands the per-GPU memory budget available for KV cache from ~62.5 GB to ~75.6 GB. What is the primary systems consequence for serving economics?
choices: The model achieves an immediate 8x reduction in inter-token latency for batch-1 decode requests by eliminating NVLink AllReduce synchronization

The maximum allowable batch size increases by more than 2.4x (from ~372 to ~900 concurrent requests), amortizing fixed weight-loading traffic across more users and driving the system from memory-bound decode toward the compute roofline
The arithmetic intensity of individual single-token operations drops by 4x, forcing the serving engine to switch to CPU execution
The node eliminates all KV cache memory allocation because INT8 keys and values are retained permanently in on-chip SRAM
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. The maximum allowable batch size increases by more than 2.4x (from ~372 to ~900 concurrent requests), amortizing fixed weight-loading traffic across more users and driving the system from memory-bound decode toward the compute roofline. Under FP16, available KV memory per GPU ($80 - 17.5 = 62.5\text{ GB}$) divided by FP16 cache per request ($0.168\text{ GB}$) permits at most $\approx 372$ concurrent requests. Quantizing weights to INT4 frees memory ($80 - 4.4 = 75.6\text{ GB}$), and halving the per-request cache to INT8 ($0.084\text{ GB}$) yields $75.6 / 0.084 \approx 900$ requests ($2.42\times$ increase). Larger batches scale arithmetic intensity ($I_{\text{decode}}(A) \propto B$), shifting decode toward the compute-bound regime and dramatically lowering serving cost per token. The other options falsely claim NVLink elimination, arithmetic intensity collapse, or permanent SRAM storage.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how precision engineering alters serving economics through memory budget reallocation and batch size expansion

focus_areas: graph compilation pipeline stages
torch.compile architecture: TorchDynamo, TorchInductor, AOTAutograd
graph breaks and CPython frame evaluation (PEP 523)
whole-program compilers (XLA) versus inference engines (TensorRT)
Triton tile-level kernel programming model
rationale.question_strategy: Test the compilation lifecycle, internal mechanisms of PyTorch tracing, performance failure modes of graph breaks, and tool selection across Triton, TensorRT, and XLA.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with pipeline execution ordering, advance to the runtime mechanics and performance traps of graph breaks, and finish with DSL/framework trade-offs.
rationale.integration: Integrates kernel fusion and memory planning into automated compiler pipelines across diverse accelerators.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Key infrastructure section covering automated compiler transformations, runtime backends, and domain-specific kernel languages.

questions.question: Consider the stages of a deep learning graph compiler optimizing a transformer feed-forward block: (1) Memory planning and buffer reuse, (2) Graph capture and intermediate representation (IR) construction, (3) Kernel selection and code generation, (4) Operator fusion and algebraic rewriting. What is the correct logical execution sequence of these stages, and why?
choices: (1) Memory planning -> (2) Graph capture -> (4) Operator fusion -> (3) Kernel selection; memory addresses must be statically locked before graph tracing can begin
(4) Operator fusion -> (2) Graph capture -> (3) Kernel selection -> (1) Memory planning; operator fusion is performed at the Python syntax level prior to graph construction
(2) Graph capture -> (3) Kernel selection -> (4) Operator fusion -> (1) Memory planning; vendor GEMM kernels must be generated before the compiler can identify fusion opportunities

(2) Graph capture -> (4) Operator fusion -> (1) Memory planning -> (3) Kernel selection; the compiler must first construct the graph, fuse adjacent operations to eliminate intermediate tensors, calculate tensor lifetimes and buffer reuse on the optimized graph, and finally lower the surviving nodes to target machine code
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. (2) Graph capture -> (4) Operator fusion -> (1) Memory planning -> (3) Kernel selection; the compiler must first construct the graph, fuse adjacent operations to eliminate intermediate tensors, calculate tensor lifetimes and buffer reuse on the optimized graph, and finally lower the surviving nodes to target machine code. The compiler cannot rewrite operations without a captured graph. Operator fusion changes tensor dependencies and eliminates intermediate buffers; performing memory planning before fusion would allocate memory for tensors that fusion subsequently deletes. Finally, kernel selection/codegen (e.g., generating Triton code or selecting cuBLAS epilogues) lowers the fused, memory-planned graph to hardware instructions. The alternative sequences violate basic compiler phase dependencies.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the logical execution sequence of graph compilation pipeline stages and justify their dependencies

questions.question: A team enables `torch.compile` on an LLM inference service with custom token validation logic and dynamic Python control flow. Profiling reveals 48 distinct graph breaks per iteration, and step latency increases by 20% compared to eager mode. What is the systems mechanism causing this performance regression?
choices: Graph breaks force TorchInductor to recompile the entire model in double-precision FP64 mode

Graph breaks fragment the computation into 48+ tiny isolated subgraphs, preventing cross-operation fusion and repeatedly dropping back to the CPython interpreter with per-subgraph dispatch and compilation overhead
Graph breaks disable GPU L2 caching, causing every memory transaction to access host CPU memory over PCIe
Graph breaks corrupt the KV cache, forcing the model to recompute prompt prefill on every decode step
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Graph breaks fragment the computation into 48+ tiny isolated subgraphs, preventing cross-operation fusion and repeatedly dropping back to the CPython interpreter with per-subgraph dispatch and compilation overhead. TorchDynamo intercepts Python bytecode; when it encounters unsupported constructs (untraceable control flow, third-party libraries), it halts tracing and inserts a graph break. Each fragment is compiled as an independent mini-graph. This breaks operator fusion across fragment boundaries, creates dozens of small kernel launches with CPU dispatch overhead, and prevents global memory planning, resulting in slower execution than eager mode. The other choices invent false claims regarding precision degradation, cache invalidation, or KV cache corruption.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose how graph breaks degrade compilation efficiency and execution throughput in dynamic PyTorch workloads

questions.question: A kernel engineer needs to implement a custom fused attention variant with a novel causal bias mask not supported in standard vendor libraries. Why is Triton generally a superior development environment for this task compared to both automated graph compilers (like TorchInductor/XLA) and hand-written raw CUDA C++?
choices: Triton exposes a tile-level programming abstraction that gives the author direct control over SRAM blocking and fusion logic while automatically handling thread block mapping, memory coalescing, and shared-memory bank conflicts
Triton bypasses the GPU memory hierarchy by executing all matrix multiplications directly inside CPU L3 cache
Triton guarantees mathematical convergence of custom loss functions through automated symbolic differentiation
Triton compiles kernels directly into FPGA bitstreams, bypassing the GPU command processor
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Triton exposes a tile-level programming abstraction that gives the author direct control over SRAM blocking and fusion logic while automatically handling thread block mapping, memory coalescing, and shared-memory bank conflicts. Automated graph compilers can only select and fuse among known library primitives, failing when an algorithm requires novel memory schedules. Raw CUDA C++ requires manual management of warp scheduling, register pressure, and shared-memory bank conflicts. Triton sits in the sweet spot: the engineer specifies block-level tiling (`BLOCK_SIZE`) to maximize SRAM reuse, while the compiler automates thread-level mechanics. The other options misrepresent Triton as a CPU cache runner, convergence verifier, or FPGA synthesizer.
questions.learning_objective: Select the appropriate abstraction level in the compiler and kernel engineering stack for custom hardware optimizations

focus_areas: speculative decoding as an arithmetic intensity transformation
acceptance rate threshold and batch dynamics
mathematical correctness via positive residual resampling
Mixture of Experts (MoE) sparse compute savings
expert parallelism, routing load imbalance, and AllToAll collective bottlenecks
rationale.question_strategy: Test the systems mechanics of algorithmic optimizations: how speculative decoding trades spare compute for bandwidth relief, the exact mathematical acceptance invariant, and MoE routing/communication trade-offs.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with speculative decoding acceptance rate economics across batch regimes, examine the exact distribution guarantee via residual sampling, and finish with MoE expert parallelism communication bottlenecks.
rationale.integration: Connects memory-bound decode physics with algorithmic interventions that alter the computational workload.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core section covering transformative algorithmic optimizations (Speculative Decoding and MoE) that rewrite the iron law budget.

questions.question: A serving team deploys speculative decoding with a 1B draft model and a 70B target model ($K=4$ draft tokens). On workload A ($B=1$, code generation with 85% acceptance), latency improves by 2.8x. On workload B ($B=64$, creative writing with 30% acceptance), latency degrades by 1.4x. What systems principles explain this divergence?
choices: At $B=64$, the draft model's parameters exceed the GPU's register file capacity, forcing all weights to spill to host CPU DRAM
Speculative decoding alters the output probability distribution on creative writing workloads, causing the model to get stuck in infinite generation loops
Code generation workloads have higher arithmetic intensity than creative writing, which forces the target model to run in FP8 precision

At $B=1$ and high acceptance, the target model's idle compute is converted into multiple accepted tokens per single weight read from HBM; at $B=64$ and low acceptance, the target model is already compute-bound, so draft compute and frequent rejected rollbacks add pure overhead
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. At $B=1$ and high acceptance, the target model's idle compute is converted into multiple accepted tokens per single weight read from HBM; at $B=64$ and low acceptance, the target model is already compute-bound, so draft compute and frequent rejected rollbacks add pure overhead. Speculative decoding works by exploiting spare Tensor Core cycles in memory-bound batch-1 decode: verifying 4 draft tokens takes roughly the same weight-streaming time as decoding 1 token. With 85% acceptance, one target pass yields ~3.5 tokens. At batch 64, decode is already compute-bound; the verification pass is no longer 'free', and with 30% acceptance, most draft work is discarded while rejected proposals force sequential corrections, slowing down the pipeline. The other choices invent false register spilling mechanisms, falsely claim distribution drift, or confuse workload semantics with arithmetic precision.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how acceptance rates and batch concurrency determine whether speculative decoding improves or degrades serving latency

questions.question: When a target model rejects a drafted token $\hat{y}_{t+i}$ during speculative decoding verification, the algorithm resamples a replacement token from the normalized positive residual distribution $(p_\theta - q_\phi)_+$. What is the critical systems and algorithmic guarantee provided by this step?
choices: It resets the draft model's KV cache, reducing its HBM footprint to zero for subsequent prompt processing
It compresses the vocabulary dimension by filtering out low-probability tokens before they reach the GPU memory bus

It mathematically guarantees that the final emitted token sequence follows the exact probability distribution $p_\theta$ of the target model, ensuring zero output quality degradation despite using an approximate draft model
It eliminates the need for the target model to execute a forward pass during subsequent verification rounds
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. It mathematically guarantees that the final emitted token sequence follows the exact probability distribution $p_\theta$ of the target model, ensuring zero output quality degradation despite using an approximate draft model. Standard speculative decoding accepts drafts with probability $\min(1, p_\theta / q_\phi)$ and resamples rejections from $(p_\theta - q_\phi)_+ / \sum_x (p_\theta(x) - q_\phi(x))_+$. This exact statistical equivalence allows systems engineers to deploy speculative decoding purely as a latency optimization without needing quality guardrails or model retraining. The other options misrepresent this mathematical proof as KV cache clearing, vocabulary pruning, or target forward pass elimination.
questions.learning_objective: Explain the mathematical acceptance and residual resampling mechanism that guarantees output equivalence in speculative decoding

questions.question: An MoE model with 64 experts is partitioned across 8 GPUs using expert parallelism. Although active parameters per token drop by 8x compared to an equivalent dense model, end-to-end step latency increases significantly under skewed production traffic. What is the primary systems bottleneck causing this regression?
choices: The gating router network requires a full dense matrix multiplication across all 64 experts for every token, consuming 90% of GPU compute
Expert parallelism duplicates the entire model parameter set on every GPU, causing catastrophic HBM out-of-memory errors

Expert parallelism routes tokens across GPUs via AllToAll collective communications; token routing skew causes severe load imbalance where popular experts become stragglers that stall all synchronized ranks
MoE layers disable CUDA stream execution, forcing all matrix multiplications to execute sequentially on the CPU
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Expert parallelism routes tokens across GPUs via AllToAll collective communications; token routing skew causes severe load imbalance where popular experts become stragglers that stall all synchronized ranks. In expert parallelism, experts are distributed across devices. Routing tokens to their assigned experts requires an AllToAll network exchange. When input tokens cluster around a few popular experts, those GPUs receive disproportionately large batches (stragglers) while other GPUs sit idle, stretching step time to the slowest rank and creating network congestion. The router itself is a lightweight projection layer (not 90% of FLOPs), expert parallelism shards parameters rather than duplicating them, and execution remains on GPU streams.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the performance trade-offs in Mixture of Experts architectures between sparse compute savings and expert-parallel AllToAll communication/imbalance costs

focus_areas: the exposed-time test for communication-computation overlap
batch size scaling of overlap budgets in tensor parallelism
CUDA streams logical concurrency and stream synchronization
SM partitioning and hardware resource interference during overlap
overlap degradation across cluster scale
rationale.question_strategy: Test the quantitative timing conditions for hiding communication, how batch size expands compute windows, and the physical resource contention that occurs when compute and communication streams execute simultaneously.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the exposed-time calculation condition, analyze batch-size dependent overlap in tensor parallelism, and finish with the physical mechanism of SM partitioning and stream interference.
rationale.integration: Connects distributed collective communication (AllReduce, NVLink) with local GPU stream scheduling and SM execution.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Key distributed performance section analyzing stream-based concurrency, overlap limits, and hardware contention.

questions.question: In a distributed training step, backward pass gradient computation takes 120 ms on GPU SMs, while gradient AllReduce synchronization takes 80 ms over the interconnect fabric. Assuming non-blocking communication is launched immediately on a separate CUDA stream, what is the resulting exposed step time for this phase, and what happens if network congestion increases AllReduce time to 150 ms?
choices: Total phase time is initially $120 + 80 = 200$ ms; when AllReduce rises to 150 ms, phase time becomes 270 ms because streams execute sequentially
Exposed communication is initially 40 ms ($120 - 80$ ms); when AllReduce rises to 150 ms, phase time becomes 30 ms
Total phase time is always exactly 80 ms because non-blocking CUDA streams terminate CPU execution as soon as the communication call is enqueued
Exposed communication is initially 0 ms (total phase time is 120 ms); when AllReduce rises to 150 ms, exposed communication becomes 30 ms (total phase time becomes 150 ms)
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Exposed communication is initially 0 ms (total phase time is 120 ms); when AllReduce rises to 150 ms, exposed communication becomes 30 ms (total phase time becomes 150 ms). Under the exposed-time test ($T_{\text{phase}} = \max(T_{\text{compute}}, T_{\text{comm}})$), when $T_{\text{comm}} = 80\text{ ms} \le T_{\text{compute}} = 120\text{ ms}$, the communication finishes before backward compute ends, leaving 0 ms of exposed communication ($T_{\text{phase}} = 120\text{ ms}$). When network congestion pushes $T_{\text{comm}}$ to 150 ms ($T_{\text{comm}} > T_{\text{compute}}$), the compute window of 120 ms hides 120 ms of transfer, leaving $150 - 120 = 30\text{ ms}$ of exposed communication time ($T_{\text{phase}} = 150\text{ ms}$). The other choices assume naive serial execution, subtract compute from communication incorrectly, or misinterpret non-blocking stream semantics.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the exposed-time test to calculate phase duration and exposed communication in overlapped distributed workloads

questions.question: In tensor-parallel inference on an 8-GPU H100 node, why does communication-computation overlap provide virtually no benefit at batch size 1, but succeed dramatically at batch size 64?
choices: At batch size 1, per-layer GEMM compute lasts only ~2 us, which is too brief to hide the fixed ~5 us AllReduce launch latency; at batch size 64, GEMM compute grows to ~20 us, creating a compute window that comfortably covers the ~7.3 us total communication time
At batch size 1, NVLink interconnect links are automatically disabled by the driver to save power
At batch size 64, tensor parallelism eliminates the need for AllReduce communication after attention and FFN blocks
At batch size 1, the GPU memory controller converts all peer-to-peer NVLink transfers into host PCIe memory copies
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. At batch size 1, per-layer GEMM compute lasts only ~2 us, which is too brief to hide the fixed ~5 us AllReduce launch latency; at batch size 64, GEMM compute grows to ~20 us, creating a compute window that comfortably covers the ~7.3 us total communication time. At $B=1$, the payload per AllReduce is tiny (32.8 KB, ~36 ns of NVLink transfer), but fixed software launch and collective synchronization overhead (~5 $\mu$s) dominates. Because local shard compute takes only ~1–2 $\mu$s, there is insufficient compute to hide behind ($T_{\text{compute}} < T_{\text{comm}}$). At $B=64$, the larger GEMMs take ~20 $\mu$s, while communication (2.1 MB transfer + launch $\approx 7.3\ \mu$s) fits entirely within the compute window ($T_{\text{compute}} > T_{\text{comm}}$). The other options invent false driver power-saving modes, claim collectives vanish, or misdescribe NVLink routing.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how batch size expands the local computation budget to enable effective communication-computation overlap in tensor parallelism

questions.question: When overlapping asynchronous NCCL AllReduce collectives with dense GEMMs across separate CUDA streams, profiling shows that peak GEMM compute throughput drops by 3–6%. What physical hardware mechanism causes this slowdown despite the operations executing on separate logical streams?
choices: The GPU hardware clock frequency is automatically halved by the thermal management unit whenever two CUDA streams are active simultaneously

NCCL communication kernels actively allocate and consume 4–8 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and memory interconnect bandwidth for packet processing and buffer copying, reducing the physical SM resources available for concurrent GEMMs
CUDA streams force the GPU instruction scheduler to serialize warp execution at the hardware thread block level
Concurrent communication corrupts the shared memory register file, forcing the GEMM to fall back to uncoalesced global memory reads
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. NCCL communication kernels actively allocate and consume 4–8 Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) and memory interconnect bandwidth for packet processing and buffer copying, reducing the physical SM resources available for concurrent GEMMs. Logical concurrency via CUDA streams does not eliminate physical hardware resource contention. On an H100 with 132 SMs, NCCL requires 4–8 SMs to manage network protocol logic, copy data to NVLink/InfiniBand staging buffers, and handle synchronization barriers (SM partitioning). Furthermore, memory traffic generated by communication contends for crossbar and L2 bandwidth, slightly degrading concurrent GEMM throughput. This 3–6% interference slowdown is minor compared to exposing the entire communication latency. The other choices invent false clock-halving rules, thread serialization claims, or register corruption bugs.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the hardware resource contention and SM partitioning mechanisms that cause interference during asynchronous stream overlap

focus_areas: the profiling hierarchy (Level 4 to Level 1 drill-down)
interpreting MFU versus MBU in memory-bound inference
timeline signature recognition in Nsight Systems traces
roofline classification from profiler counters
the Heisenberg effect in profiling and the iterative feedback loop
rationale.question_strategy: Test practical diagnostic workflows: interpreting diverging MFU/MBU signals, navigating the profiling hierarchy to locate root causes, and recognizing launch-bound trace patterns.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with metric interpretation (MFU vs MBU in decode), advance to hierarchical diagnostic sequencing, and finish with timeline pattern recognition in Nsight Systems traces.
rationale.integration: Synthesizes roofline modeling, memory wall diagnosis, and kernel optimization into an evidence-driven measurement discipline.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Core practical section establishing the measurement hierarchy, profiler tools, metric interpretation, and trace diagnosis.

questions.question: An engineer profiling an autoregressive LLM decode service on an H100 GPU measures 3% Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) alongside 88% Model Bandwidth Utilization (MBU). How should this profile signature be interpreted, and what is the appropriate engineering response?
choices: The system has a critical performance bug because MFU and MBU must always track within 5% of each other on modern Tensor Core accelerators
The kernel is compute-bound, so the engineer should hand-tune Tensor Core warp scheduling to increase MFU toward 80%
The profiler is malfunctioning because achieving an MBU above 50% on an H100 GPU violates hardware safety guardrails

The implementation is healthy and operating near the physical memory bandwidth ceiling; low MFU is the expected signature of memory-bound batch-1 decode, and gains must come from reducing bytes moved (quantization, fusion) or increasing batch size
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. The implementation is healthy and operating near the physical memory bandwidth ceiling; low MFU is the expected signature of memory-bound batch-1 decode, and gains must come from reducing bytes moved (quantization, fusion) or increasing batch size. In batch-1 autoregressive decode, arithmetic intensity is ~1 FLOP/byte, far below the H100 FP16 ridge point (~295 FLOP/byte). The GPU reaches 88% of its 3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth limit while consuming only a tiny fraction of its 989 TFLOP/s compute peak. Treating low MFU as an implementation defect misdiagnoses a memory-bound workload as compute-bound. Further FLOP scheduling will yield zero gain; improvements require shrinking bytes transferred per token (INT4 quantization, KV compression) or increasing batch size to raise arithmetic intensity. The other choices misinterpret memory-bound physics or invent false metric tracking rules.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret divergent MFU and MBU profiling metrics to correctly identify memory-bound inference regimes

questions.question: A production serving cluster experiences a 3x increase in P99 latency. An engineer immediately begins tuning the assembly instructions of the primary GEMM kernel using Nsight Compute. Why does this violate the profiling hierarchy principle?
choices: Nsight Compute can only be executed on CPU clusters and cannot record GPU instructions

Nsight Compute inspects local Level 1 kernel execution; jumping directly to kernel tuning risks wasting effort on an already-optimal kernel when the true root cause may be Level 4 queueing, Level 3 distributed stragglers, or Level 2 CPU launch gaps
GEMM kernels are mathematically incapable of causing latency regressions in production workloads
The profiling hierarchy requires developers to modify CUDA kernel source code before collecting any application telemetry
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Nsight Compute inspects local Level 1 kernel execution; jumping directly to kernel tuning risks wasting effort on an already-optimal kernel when the true root cause may be Level 4 queueing, Level 3 distributed stragglers, or Level 2 CPU launch gaps. The profiling hierarchy dictates a top-down drill-down: start at Level 4 (Application metrics: TTFT, ITL, queue depth, P99), descend to Level 3 (Distributed: AllReduce synchronization, straggler nodes), move to Level 2 (Trace: Nsight Systems timeline, launch gaps, CPU-GPU sync), and only inspect Level 1 (Kernel: Nsight Compute register usage, memory coalescing) if a specific kernel is proven to be the critical-path bottleneck. Optimizing a GEMM that takes 5 ms is futile if requests are spending 100 ms waiting in an upstream network queue. The other options misstate Nsight Compute capabilities or invert diagnostic methodology.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the top-down profiling hierarchy to diagnose system performance degradations from global symptoms to local causes

questions.question: In an Nsight Systems timeline trace of a transformer model, the CUDA API row displays continuous CPU dispatch activity while the CUDA HW row shows dozens of narrow, microsecond-duration kernel bars separated by repeated empty gaps. What is the diagnosis and primary optimization intervention?
choices: The workload is compute-bound; the primary intervention is to upgrade to a GPU with higher peak TFLOP/s
The workload is experiencing thermal throttling; the primary intervention is to reduce GPU fan speed limits

The workload is launch-bound, meaning the CPU cannot enqueue kernels fast enough to keep GPU SMs occupied; the primary intervention is graph compilation with `torch.compile` or CUDA Graphs to eliminate per-kernel dispatch overhead
The workload is network-bound; the primary intervention is to replace InfiniBand switches with Ethernet routers
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. The workload is launch-bound, meaning the CPU cannot enqueue kernels fast enough to keep GPU SMs occupied; the primary intervention is graph compilation with `torch.compile` or CUDA Graphs to eliminate per-kernel dispatch overhead. In PyTorch eager mode, each kernel launch incurs 5–20 $\mu$s of CPU dispatch latency (Python interpreter, GIL, CUDA driver). When a layer consists of many small operations (LayerNorm, GELU, residual adds) that execute in 1–3 $\mu$s, the GPU completes each kernel before the CPU can dispatch the next, producing empty idle gaps on the CUDA HW timeline. CUDA Graphs and `torch.compile(mode="reduce-overhead")` eliminate this dispatch bottleneck by recording the sequence once and replaying the entire graph with a single launch command (~5 $\mu$s). The other options misidentify launch overhead as compute, thermal, or network bottlenecks.
questions.learning_objective: Identify launch-bound execution patterns from Nsight Systems timeline traces and select appropriate graph capture remedies

focus_areas: Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) vs raw hardware utilization at fleet scale
the scaling tax formula: 1 - (Fleet MFU / Local MFU)
gray failures and single-straggler synchronization propagation
hierarchical and targeted profiling at cluster scale
the hero run tax in capacity planning
rationale.question_strategy: Test fleet-level performance measurement discipline: distinguishing useful model progress from busy cycles, calculating the scaling tax, and analyzing straggler propagation in synchronous distributed execution.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with contrasting hardware busyness against useful MFU, move to calculating the scaling tax and diagnosing straggler propagation, and finish with capacity planning realities.
rationale.integration: Extends single-node profiling into cluster-wide distributed training and serving efficiency metrics.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Essential operational section addressing multi-node measurement, scaling tax quantification, and gray failure detection.

questions.question: A 512-GPU distributed training cluster reports 95% GPU hardware utilization across all nodes, but fleet-wide Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) is measured at only 32% (a drop from 64% measured on an 8-GPU single-node canary). Which explanation correctly accounts for this discrepancy?
choices: Hardware utilization counts any time the SMs are busy (including wasted cycles on gradient checkpointing recomputation, padding, communication bubbles, and synchronization stalls), whereas MFU measures only FLOPs that directly advance model convergence
Hardware utilization measures memory bandwidth while MFU measures compute throughput, so the two metrics naturally diverge in distributed training
The 95% hardware utilization confirms the cluster is operating optimally, indicating that MFU is an unreliable metric for multi-node clusters
The InfiniBand network fabric has disabled GPU Tensor Cores, forcing the cluster to execute matrix multiplications in integer mode
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Hardware utilization counts any time the SMs are busy (including wasted cycles on gradient checkpointing recomputation, padding, communication bubbles, and synchronization stalls), whereas MFU measures only FLOPs that directly advance model convergence. Raw hardware utilization (e.g., from `nvidia-smi`) merely checks whether an SM has active warps. If a distributed run spends time executing activation recomputation, spinning on barrier locks, or executing uncoalesced memory transfers, the hardware is '100% busy' but accomplishing zero useful model training. MFU isolates the algorithmic FLOPs required by the forward/backward passes divided by peak hardware throughput ($N \cdot R_{\text{peak}} \cdot t_{\text{step}}$), exposing the true scaling tax. The other choices confuse metric definitions, dismiss MFU, or invent impossible network-driven hardware disabling.
questions.learning_objective: Contrast raw hardware utilization with Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) to detect wasted computation at fleet scale

questions.question: A foundation model pretraining run achieves 65% MFU on an 8-GPU node (step time = 180 ms). When scaled to a 128-GPU cluster, step time increases to 245 ms for equivalent per-GPU token throughput, dropping MFU to 48%. A single node in the cluster has a degraded PCIe connection causing its backward pass to run 15% slower than the rest. What is the cluster scaling tax, and how does this single node affect fleet efficiency?
choices: The scaling tax is $1 - (48 / 65) \approx 26.2\%$; in synchronous distributed execution, the single slow node acts as a global straggler at AllReduce barriers, forcing all 127 healthy nodes to wait and degrading entire fleet MFU
The scaling tax is $65\% - 48\% = 17.0\%$; the slow node only affects its own local batch while the other 127 nodes complete their steps independently without delay
The scaling tax is $245 / 180 = 1.36\times$; the slow node causes 50% data loss across the training dataset
The scaling tax is 0% because distributed training frameworks automatically rebalance compute to bypass slow PCIe nodes
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. The scaling tax is $1 - (48 / 65) \approx 26.2\%$; in synchronous distributed execution, the single slow node acts as a global straggler at AllReduce barriers, forcing all 127 healthy nodes to wait and degrading entire fleet MFU. The scaling tax is the relative loss in efficiency: $1 - (\text{Fleet MFU} / \text{Local MFU}) = 1 - (0.48 / 0.65) \approx 26.2\%$. In synchronous data-parallel or tensor-parallel training, every step concludes with a global collective synchronization (AllReduce). A 'gray failure'—such as a single node with degraded PCIe or thermal throttling that runs 15% slower—delays the collective barrier, forcing all other nodes to sit idle waiting for the straggler and dragging down the entire 128-GPU cluster's MFU. The other choices miscalculate the relative scaling tax, misunderstand synchronous barrier physics, or invent automated rebalancing capabilities.
questions.learning_objective: Calculate the distributed scaling tax and analyze how gray-failure stragglers propagate efficiency losses across synchronized fleets

questions.question: An engineering organization plans data center GPU capacity for a 30-day foundation model pretraining run based on published MLPerf benchmark results that report 65% MFU on identical hardware. In production, the training run takes 37.5 days. What operational factors explain this 'hero run tax'?
choices: Production GPU drivers introduce a mandatory 20% artificial delay on non-benchmark binaries to protect electrical grids
MLPerf benchmarks execute floating-point operations on synthetic data that compresses 10x better in GPU registers than real-world text tokens

Benchmark hero runs strip out essential production overheads (continuous observability logging, periodic checkpointing, health heartbeats) and run on freshly rebooted, isolated hardware free from multi-tenant network noise or thermal degradation
Production PyTorch installations disable Tensor Cores unless a specific enterprise licensing flag is passed at runtime
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Benchmark hero runs strip out essential production overheads (continuous observability logging, periodic checkpointing, health heartbeats) and run on freshly rebooted, isolated hardware free from multi-tenant network noise or thermal degradation. Industry benchmarks represent carefully tuned, pristine configurations designed to showcase peak capability. Real production environments must pay the operational tax: saving gigabytes of checkpoint state to persistent storage, streaming telemetry, handling multi-tenant InfiniBand network jitter, and managing thermal throttling over weeks of sustained execution. A 10–20% gap between benchmark MFU and production MFU ($30\text{ days} / (1 - 0.20) = 37.5\text{ days}$) is expected, and capacity planning must explicitly budget for this reality tax. The other choices invent absurd driver throttling, synthetic data compression, or licensing myths.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the operational factors causing the gap between benchmark hero runs and sustained production fleet efficiency

focus_areas: the 4-step diagnostic optimization sequence
compounding and sub-multiplicative speedup interactions
sequencing passive before active interventions
the 70B LLM case study optimization rounds (precision -> fusion/compiler -> speculation)
adaptive speculative decoding policies under varying load
rationale.question_strategy: Test the systematic sequencing and compounding interaction of performance techniques: baseline measurement, bottleneck-guided intervention ordering, sub-multiplicative returns due to shifting bottlenecks, and adaptive serving policies.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the diagnostic playbook sequence, move to analyzing sub-multiplicative compounding and bottleneck displacement, and finish with case-study serving policy design.
rationale.integration: Integrates memory wall, fusion, precision, compilation, and speculative decoding into a comprehensive end-to-end engineering workflow.
rationale.ranking_explanation: Capstone application section demonstrating the end-to-end diagnostic sequence and compounding optimization rounds on a 70B model.

questions.question: A performance team is tasked with optimizing a raw, unoptimized 70B LLM serving pipeline on an 8-GPU H100 node that is deeply memory-bound at batch size 1. Following the chapter's playbook heuristic of applying passive/low-effort optimizations before active/complex ones, which sequence represents the recommended order of interventions?
choices: Hand-write custom CUDA GEMM kernels -> Deploy speculative decoding -> Apply INT4 quantization -> Collect baseline profile traces

Baseline profiling -> INT4 weight & INT8 KV cache quantization (to relieve HBM traffic and expand batch capacity) -> FlashAttention & `torch.compile` with CUDA Graphs (to fuse element-wise ops and eliminate launch gaps) -> Adaptive speculative decoding (for low-load latency reduction)
Deploy speculative decoding immediately -> Double model parameter count with MoE -> Enable CUDA Graphs on variable-length prefill -> Measure throughput
Apply INT1 binary quantization -> Rewrite serving stack in C++ -> Enable `torch.compile` -> Profile baseline
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Baseline profiling -> INT4 weight & INT8 KV cache quantization (to relieve HBM traffic and expand batch capacity) -> FlashAttention & `torch.compile` with CUDA Graphs (to fuse element-wise ops and eliminate launch gaps) -> Adaptive speculative decoding (for low-load latency reduction). The playbook establishes a strict diagnostic discipline: measure baseline first to identify the primary bottleneck (memory bandwidth and KV capacity). Next, apply high-impact precision engineering (AWQ INT4 + INT8 KV) to address the dominant weight-streaming bottleneck and enable larger batch sizes. Once batching shifts the workload, apply compiler fusion (`torch.compile` + CUDA Graphs) and FlashAttention to clean up element-wise and launch overheads. Finally, evaluate complex algorithmic additions like speculative decoding only if latency targets remain unmet. Starting with hand-tuned kernels, speculative decoding, or architecture changes without profiling violates the diagnostic sequence.
questions.learning_objective: Design and sequence a multi-round optimization plan following the chapter's diagnostic playbook

questions.question: In the 70B serving case study, INT4 weight quantization in isolation delivers a 2.6x throughput improvement, and `torch.compile` with FlashAttention in isolation delivers a 1.8x improvement. When applied together, their combined throughput gain is 3.75x rather than the multiplicative product ($2.6 \times 1.8 = 4.68\text{x}$). What systems principle explains this sub-multiplicative result?
choices: FlashAttention and INT4 quantization interfere numerically, causing Tensor Cores to discard half of all executed matrix multiplications
`torch.compile` disables weight quantization kernels, forcing the model to reload weights in full FP16 precision
The GPU hardware clock automatically downclocks by 25% whenever multiple software optimizations are active simultaneously

Optimizations shift the active bottleneck among memory bandwidth, compute throughput, and launch overhead; once INT4 quantization relieves HBM bandwidth pressure and enables larger batches, the workload becomes partially compute-bound, reducing the headroom available for subsequent memory-reduction techniques
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Optimizations shift the active bottleneck among memory bandwidth, compute throughput, and launch overhead; once INT4 quantization relieves HBM bandwidth pressure and enables larger batches, the workload becomes partially compute-bound, reducing the headroom available for subsequent memory-reduction techniques. Optimization is a waterbed problem. When INT4 quantization slashes weight-read traffic by 4x and enables batch size 32, arithmetic intensity climbs and the system transitions from deeply memory-bound to partially compute-bound. At that point, techniques that primarily target memory traffic (like FlashAttention) or launch overhead operate on a smaller remaining fraction of step time. Speedups across technique families are sub-multiplicative because each intervention alters the dominant term in the iron law. The other choices invent false numerical interference, compiler disabling bugs, or clock downclocking myths.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how bottleneck shifts among memory-, compute-, and overhead-bound regimes cause compounding speedups to be sub-multiplicative

questions.question: In Round 3 of the 70B case study, the serving stack implements an adaptive speculative decoding policy that enables speculation only when active batch size is below 8, falling back to standard autoregressive decode at higher batch sizes. Why is this adaptive policy necessary for optimal production operation?
choices: Speculative decoding causes CUDA out-of-memory crashes if active batch size exceeds 8 due to draft model weight expansion

At low batch sizes, decode is memory-bound with idle Tensor Cores available for draft generation and parallel verification; at high batch sizes, the GPU approaches compute saturation, making draft compute and verification overhead degrade aggregate throughput
FlashAttention-2 is mathematically incompatible with speculative decoding whenever concurrent batch size exceeds 8
The draft model requires a dedicated physical GPU that cannot be shared with batches larger than 8 requests
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. At low batch sizes, decode is memory-bound with idle Tensor Cores available for draft generation and parallel verification; at high batch sizes, the GPU approaches compute saturation, making draft compute and verification overhead degrade aggregate throughput. Speculative decoding trades spare compute for latency reduction. At $B=1$, the target model has ample idle FLOP/s waiting on HBM weight reads, so verifying candidate tokens is virtually 'free' in wall-clock time, reducing ITL from 32 ms to 10.3 ms. At $B=32$, the workload is compute-saturated; draft model execution and target verification compete directly for Tensor Core cycles, adding compute overhead without proportional latency benefit and lowering aggregate throughput. An adaptive threshold maintains low latency under light traffic and high throughput under heavy traffic. The other options invent false OOM crash rules, FlashAttention incompatibilities, or dedicated GPU hardware requirements.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate when speculative decoding should be dynamically enabled or bypassed based on batch concurrency and compute saturation

measuring throughput in isolation from quality and tail latency
rationale.question_strategy: Test the ability to recognize pervasive industry anti-patterns: misattributing inference speed to FLOP/s, over-optimizing the largest GEMM kernel while ignoring the long tail of overhead, and sacrificing tail latency for average throughput.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Start with the hardware spec sheet FLOP/s fallacy, move to Amdahl's law on the non-GEMM long tail, and conclude with the trade-off between throughput and P99 tail latency.

questions.question: A team upgrades their LLM serving infrastructure from A100 GPUs to an accelerator featuring 3x higher advertised peak FP16 TFLOP/s, expecting an immediate 3x reduction in single-user generation latency. In production, inter-token latency improves by only 12%. What core systems fallacy explains this disappointment?
choices: Assuming that peak FLOP/s dictates inference latency, when single-user ($B=1$) decode is strictly memory-bound; because memory bandwidth only increased modestly between the chips, token generation remained capped by HBM streaming speed
Failing to enable FP64 double-precision mode, which is required to unlock the new accelerator's Tensor Cores
Assuming that the A100 and the new accelerator share the same PCIe bus topology, which disabled NVLink
Neglecting to realize that single-user LLM inference is strictly bounded by disk I/O read speeds rather than GPU memory bandwidth
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Assuming that peak FLOP/s dictates inference latency, when single-user ($B=1$) decode is strictly memory-bound; because memory bandwidth only increased modestly between the chips, token generation remained capped by HBM streaming speed. As established by the roofline model, batch-1 decode has an arithmetic intensity of ~1 FLOP/byte, sitting orders of magnitude below the ridge point of modern GPUs. In this regime, execution time is determined by $D_{\text{vol}} / \text{BW}$ (reading model weights from HBM). An accelerator with 3x higher TFLOP/s but similar memory bandwidth leaves the dominant weight-streaming term untouched; the arithmetic units simply idle faster. Upgrading peak compute only accelerates compute-bound large-batch serving or training. The other choices invent false FP64 requirements, irrelevant PCIe topology assumptions, or absurd disk I/O claims for resident models.
questions.learning_objective: Critique the fallacy that peak hardware compute throughput (FLOP/s) dictates single-request inference generation latency

questions.question: An engineer profiles an LLM decode step where the primary GEMM kernel accounts for 40% of step time, while the remaining 60% is split across 50 small element-wise kernels, LayerNorms, and launch gaps. The engineer spends a month hand-tuning the GEMM kernel to be 2x faster. What is the maximum overall step speedup achieved, and why was this an inefficient investment?
choices: Overall speedup is 2.00x, because accelerating the primary matrix multiplication automatically scales all dependent normalization layers
Overall speedup is 0.50x, because hand-tuning low-level GEMM kernels causes compiler de-optimization in surrounding PyTorch code
Overall speedup is 1.67x, because the GEMM kernel represents the entire mathematical foundation of the forward pass

Overall speedup is at most 1.25x (step time drops from 100% to $60\% + 20\% = 80\%$), because Amdahl's law limits gains when the unaddressed 60% long tail of launch gaps and element-wise kernels dominates execution
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Overall speedup is at most 1.25x (step time drops from 100% to $60\% + 20\% = 80\%$), because Amdahl's law limits gains when the unaddressed 60% long tail of launch gaps and element-wise kernels dominates execution. This illustrates the 'single largest kernel' fallacy. Halving the 40% GEMM slice reduces it to 20%, leaving total step time at $60\% + 20\% = 80\%$ ($1.0 / 0.80 = 1.25\times$ speedup). The engineer ignored the 60% long tail of small operations (LayerNorm, GELU, residual adds, dispatch overhead). Applying automated graph compilation (`torch.compile`) or CUDA Graphs would have attacked that 60% slice directly with far less engineering effort. The other choices violate Amdahl's law or invent false compiler de-optimization mechanisms.
questions.learning_objective: Apply Amdahl's law to avoid the single-largest-kernel trap when optimizing ML execution pipelines

questions.question: A serving team increases mean token throughput from 500 to 900 tokens/second by implementing aggressive dynamic batching, but customer satisfaction collapses because P99 inter-token latency spikes from 45 ms to 650 ms. What systems mechanism caused this production failure?
choices: High throughput caused the GPU to drop network packets over the InfiniBand fabric
Dynamic batching forced the model to execute all forward passes in FP32 precision, slowing down the GPU

Maximizing average throughput packed large, variable-length requests into common execution batches, creating head-of-line blocking, KV cache memory reallocation stalls, and tail latency degradation for interactive users
P99 latency is an artificial synthetic metric that does not reflect actual user experience in production
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Maximizing average throughput packed large, variable-length requests into common execution batches, creating head-of-line blocking, KV cache memory reallocation stalls, and tail latency degradation for interactive users. This highlights the pitfall of optimizing average throughput while ignoring tail latency. Large batch sizes raise arithmetic intensity and maximize GPU token throughput, but grouping requests of widely varying sequence lengths forces short requests to wait for long requests to finish (head-of-line blocking). Furthermore, aggressive batching strains the memory allocator, causing dynamic KV cache page allocation pauses. For interactive applications, user perception is dominated by the P99 tail latency SLA, not the mean. Production serving requires balancing throughput against strict tail-latency budgets. The other choices invent false network packet loss, precision downgrades, or dismiss tail latency.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the architectural tension between maximizing aggregate serving throughput and maintaining strict P99 tail-latency SLOs
